   Haze in 2026 estimated to cost Singapore $2.32 billion, up 4% from 2015: Experts
 Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox
 Understanding who bears the cost of haze can help Singapore target protection and plan adaptation, experts say. 
 ST PHOTO: BRIAN TEO
 Elysia Tan
 Published   Nov 08, 2026, 06:39 PM
 Updated   Nov 08, 2026, 09:14 PM
 Set as preferred source Listen 中文 SINGAPORE – The 2026 haze episode – the worst in more than a decade – has cost Singapore’s economy $2.32 billion as at Oct 31, about 4% higher than in 2015.
 The figure comes from a preliminary estimate by Nanyang Technological University’s (NTU) Euston Quah and Singapore University of Social Sciences’ (SUSS) Eugene Or.
 “The sheer scale of this damage strengthens the case for funding prevention alongside tougher penalties,” they argued.
 The 2026 estimate builds on a published, peer-reviewed cost framework created by Quah, NTU’s Chia Wai Mun and SUSS’ Tan Tsiat Siong in 2015.
 They had estimated the 2015 haze costs to be $1.83 billion, or $2.23 billion in September 2026 prices.
 Quah and Or arrived at the larger bill for 2026 despite fewer hazy days and a lower average Pollutant Standards Index reading. The professors attributed this to a larger population, higher incomes and visitor spending, and updated health data and assumptions.
 The health burden, which includes treatment bills, the value of reducing the risk of illness and premature death, was higher in 2026 than in 2015.
 Tourism losses – both direct and additional business losses – were also higher in 2026 than 11 years ago, taking into consideration arrivals as well as spending data.
 Disruption was also reflected in lost time due to illness, whether for work or non-work activities. The 2026 cost was lower than in 2015, as fewer hazy days and lower pollution outweighed higher earnings and population growth.
 Another cost component considered was protection, such as masks, which fell from 2015 levels. Household growth was offset by the shorter haze duration.
 The calculations also factored in well-being, taking into consideration people’s willingness to pay for cleaner air.
 Complementary approaches
 Measuring haze losses should guide action, Quah and Or said, adding that understanding who bears the cost can help Singapore target protection and plan adaptation.
 The data can also be used to pursue cost-sharing with Indonesia and affected countries to prevent burning.
 While the law can help prevent fires by changing what businesses stand to lose, the professors also suggested a complementary “victim-pays” approach, where affected countries help finance prevention by making alternatives to burning more affordable.
 “If supporting fire-free practices costs less than the damage avoided, contributing can leave these countries better off,” they said.
 But they also acknowledged that this raises concerns about fairness, and that while public money should fund measurable reductions in fire risk, companies responsible should still be held accountable.
 “Each proposal still requires a thorough cost-benefit analysis,” they said, noting that measuring haze losses provides a starting point for decision-making.
 “A $2.32 billion haze bill does not automatically justify a $2.32 billion prevention budget,” Quah and Or added, suggesting phased funding based on results.
 “Measuring haze damage helps Singapore decide where action could make the greatest difference.” THE BUSINESS TIMES
